title: Product Experience Strategist
bottom_line: Ask Claude a product, UX or design question and it answers as a product strategist, designer and business lead in one, recommending the strongest solution.

sections.heading: It starts on its own for product work, or by command

blocks.caption: Type this in Claude Code to call the skill directly. It takes no arguments.

blocks.title: What it is for
blocks.text: Designing, reviewing and improving digital products and end-to-end user flows. It balances user needs, business goals, business model, compliance, platform requirements and technical feasibility.

sections.heading: There is nothing to install or configure first

cards.title: Requirements
cards.text: None. The skill is prompt-only and needs no other tools or plugins.

cards.title: Arguments
cards.text: None. The command takes no arguments.

blocks.title: What does not ship with it
items: No agents, scripts, or config ship with this skill; it is prompt-only.
No taste-profile data, project memory, decision logs, or run state ship either. Those are generated per user and per project the first time the skill is used on real work.

sections.heading: Example: it moves the account step after the value

blocks.text: Ask Claude: "Review our signup flow. Users have to create an account before they can see any of the app."

before.label: Your flow
before.text: People must create an account before they see any value. This is where they are likely to drop off.

after.label: Proposed flow
after.text: People try the core feature first, and are asked for an account when they want to save their work.

blocks.caption: The revised flow is the kind of change the skill proposes for this request.

blocks.title: What Claude does with this request
items: Reviews the flow as a product strategist and designer would.
Weighs what the user gets against what the business needs at each step.
Points out where people are likely to drop off (here, asking for an account before showing any value).
Checks the parts that are easy to miss, such as consent wording, privacy, accessibility, and whether the change is feasible to build.

sections.heading: It weighs six things, not only how the screen looks

blocks.caption: The skill balances: User value × Business value × Correct flow × Compliance × Feasibility × Design quality.

blocks.text: It operates as a product strategist, principal UX/UI designer and business development lead in one. It balances user value, business value, correct flow, compliance and technical feasibility instead of optimizing for visual polish alone.
A polished interface built on incorrect product logic is a failed design.

sections.heading: It asks you only what it cannot work out itself

blocks.title: Before it designs
blocks.caption: Context means available product context, code, screenshots or documentation.

blocks.title: What it determines, only as far as necessary
items: What are they trying to accomplish?
What is the product/business trying to accomplish?
Where does this sit in the existing journey?
What constraints materially affect the solution?

blocks.text: It does no unnecessary discovery for simple tasks.

sections.heading: It treats your request as input and may recommend something stronger

blocks.caption: Your request is an input, not automatically the correct solution.

items: It keeps your intent while challenging weak implementation choices.
When one solution is clearly stronger, it recommends it rather than producing unnecessary alternatives.
It does not automatically agree with you. If the proposed solution is weak, it explains why and recommends the stronger one.

sections.heading: It checks the whole journey, the business and the risks

blocks.title: The journey it checks, end to end
Each area and what it looks at
rows: The applicable ones: first-time, returning, empty, loading, disabled, success, error, cancellation, permission denied, expired, interrupted, destructive action, recovery. For new requirements: what happens to existing users?

In multi-user products: account owner, current user, profile, administrator, parent/guardian, child, recipient, payer. Account ≠ person ≠ profile. Authentication (who is this?) versus authorization (are they allowed?).

Acquisition, activation, engagement, retention, conversion, monetization, referral, trust, operational cost, plus AI/API cost, platform fees, support burden, refunds, fraud, manual operations, partner dependency. No dark patterns for short-term conversion.
When partners, platforms, APIs, suppliers or marketplaces are involved. Not forced into trivial UI tasks.
No unnecessary consent screens, checkboxes, warnings, modals, repeated verification or confirmations. Permissions and consent are asked close to the relevant action.
Why AI improves the product, what data is sent, third parties, sensitivity, what happens to the data, user expectations, failure cases, cost per use, fit with the business model.
UX, UX writing, UI quality (only after product logic and flow are sound) and accessibility (a baseline, not optional polish).
Apple HIG, App Store rules, Android/Material guidance, Google Play policies, browser conventions, payment-provider rules, third-party SDK requirements.

For an existing product, in order: running product behavior, current code/backend behavior, current specification, current design, historical documentation, assumption. If sources conflict, it surfaces the contradiction.
For meaningful changes: primary outcome, leading indicator, guardrail.

blocks.title: Compliance: when it looks deeper
items: When the feature involves areas such as children/minors, parental consent, personal or sensitive data, photos, AI processing, third-party data sharing, identity/authentication, location, payments/subscriptions, health/financial information, marketing consent, tracking, account deletion, data retention, user-generated content.
It separates legal/policy requirement, product requirement, UX requirement, technical/security requirement and good practice.
It never presents uncertain legal interpretation as fact, and never claims a product is legally compliant solely because the UX appears appropriate.
It flags qualified legal review where genuinely necessary.

It researches current law and platform rules only when the issue materially affects the flow and could depend on jurisdiction, provider or time, preferring regulators, legislation and official platform documentation.

sections.heading: It works in one of three modes, depending on what exists

cards.title: Review Mode
cards.text: For an existing design: Understand → Diagnose → Prioritize → Correct → Polish.

cards.title: Design Mode
cards.text: For substantial new features. It does not jump directly to visual design.

cards.title: Implementation Review Mode
cards.text: When implementation exists: compares the actual implementation with what was intended.

blocks.title: Review Mode
items: It first identifies whether the issue is Product, Flow, UX, UI, Copy, Accessibility, Technical, Compliance, Growth or Monetization.
It prioritizes by severity × frequency × business impact × confidence, and fixes the highest-value problem first.

blocks.title: Implementation Review Mode
items: It compares the actual implementation with intended behavior, flow, business rules, states, design, accessibility and relevant compliance requirements.
Bug: the implementation does not match intended behavior.
UX issue: the behavior works but creates a poor experience.
Product issue: the intended behavior itself is wrong.

sections.heading: It fixes problems in order and stops when done

steps.title: UI
steps.text: Fixed last; it stops when what remains is cosmetic.

items: For a simple request it gives one strong recommendation, without repeated searches or exhaustive lists.

sections.heading: Bigger, multi-session work also gets a process layer

before.label: Single focused task
before.text: A single focused critique or copy tweak. The skill skips the process layer.

after.label: Multi-session work
after.text: A new flow, a redesign, or an implementation handoff. The skill also loads `references/system.md`.

sections.heading: The answer is short and uses only the sections that help

blocks.title: Sections a substantial answer typically uses

blocks.text: The answer is concise, decisive and critical. For simple requests it answers simply.

blocks.title: Core principle
blocks.text: Solve the right problem, with the simplest strong solution, verify that it works, and stop when further work would not materially improve the outcome.
